deep.reconstruction:
The page has two layers.

(A) LEFT COLUMN: a mathematical table. It continues, for the primes 211 to 433, the table begun on the previous page, which covered p = 3 to 199. Each row has the form 'p . a . b | c'.

- b = (p-1)/ord_p(10). This is the number of distinct periods of the decimal expansions of k/p. I checked this on many rows, all in agreement:
  - 211: ord 30, b = 7.
  - 239: ord 7, b = 34.
  - 241: ord 30, b = 8.
  - 251: ord 50, b = 5.
  - 271: ord 5, b = 54.
  - 281: ord 28, b = 10.
  - 331: ord 110, b = 3.
  - 349: ord 116, b = 3.
  - 353: ord 32, b = 11.
  - 397: ord 99, b = 4.
  - 401: ord 200, b = 2.
  - 421: ord 140, b = 3.
- '* 1' marks primes for which 10 is itself a primitive root (b = 1, a = 10). These are 223, 229, 233, 257, 263, 269, 313, 337, 367, 379, 383, 389, 419, 433, exactly the full-reptend primes in this range.
- a is a primitive root g chosen so that g^b ≡ 10 (mod p), i.e. ind_g(10) = b, as small as possible. Checked by hand:
  - 7^2 = 49, 7^3 ≡ 132, 7^4 ≡ 80, 7^7 ≡ 132·80 = 10560 ≡ 10 (mod 211).
  - 28^11 ≡ 10 (mod 353). On the previous page, 17^2 ≡ 10 (mod 31) and 5^12 ≡ 10 (mod 37).
- c is ind_g(2). On the previous page the full lists are ind 2, ind 3, ind 5, ind 7, ... For example, for p = 11, g = 2 they read 1, 8, 4, 7. From p = 89 onward only ind 2 is entered.
  - Check: for 223 (g = 10), 10^3 ≡ 108, 10^6 ≡ 68, 10^9 ≡ -15, 10^18 ≡ 225 ≡ 2. So ind 2 = 18, as written.
  - Parity and order checks pass where tried: 257 gives 80, a multiple of 16; 337 gives 304, a multiple of 16; 211 gives 139, odd, since 2 is a non-residue.
- Some rows carry two numbers: 239 (158, 206), 241 (50, 202), 271 (154, 117), 401 (98, 373). The second is possibly the index of another small prime, or a correction.

Purpose. This is Gauss's device of Disquisitiones Arithmeticae art. 72 and 316ff. Choosing the primitive root so that ind 10 equals the number of periods makes an index table double as a table for converting common fractions into decimals. These are exactly the bases of DA Table I (13 → 6, 31 → 17, 37 → 5, 41 → 6, 43 → 28, ...). The page title 'TENTAMEN THEORIAE RESIDVORVM' (an early working title of the DA) dates it to c. 1796-98.

Small marginal notes:
- '7.3.2.2', '11.5.3.2', '13.3.2.4', '31.5.2', '29.3.2.2', '61.3.2', with numbers like 6, 10, 12, 28, 30 (= p-1) beneath them. These look like similar order data for other bases, e.g. ord_7(2) = 3 with 6/3 = 2, and ord_11(3) = 5 with 10/5 = 2. This reading is speculative.
- Two subtractions are correct: 554 - 420 = 134 and 388 - 204 = 184.

(B) CENTRE AND RIGHT: non-mathematical or obscure material.
- Pen trials of the name 'GAUSS / GAVSS', partly written upside down.
- The title 'TENTAMEN THEORIAE RESIDVORVM' and Latin fragments ('V cum variis a', 'fons Blandusiae' from Horace, Odes III.13).
- Many profile sketches and a framed portrait head.
- A tally-like numeric scheme '5-pl. 6,7,10,11,11' with rows 1-6 and partial sums (55, 66, 128, 109, 404, ...); its meaning is unclear and possibly not mathematical.
- Stray jottings such as '2^43', '√2 = 3/39', '392+9', '3/14', '260/620', '203/443'; their meaning is unclear.
errors: Row 359: the transcription reads a = '399', which is impossible (it must be < 359). The digit is misread or miswritten in the image, so the base for 359 needs re-reading.
Row 241: of the two numbers 50 and 202, only 50 can be ind_g(2). ord_241(2) = 24, so ind 2 must be a multiple of 10. The 202 must therefore be something else (another index, or a correction).
The stray '√2 = 3/39' is not a correct statement on any obvious reading. It is probably a doodle or shorthand, not a claim.
The central tally (55, 66, 128, 109, 404, etc.) cannot be verified, as its meaning is unclear.

results.what: For each prime p in 211..433: the period count b = (p-1)/ord_p(10), a primitive root g with g^b ≡ 10 (mod p), and ind_g(2).
results.modern_name: Table of indices (discrete logarithms) with primitive roots normalized by ind(10) = number of decimal periods; multiplicative order of 10 / full-reptend primes
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), art. 72, 312-318 and Tables I and III; index tables also by Euler, and later Jacobi (Canon Arithmeticus, 1839)

results.what: Identification of primes for which 10 is a primitive root (the '*1' rows).
results.modern_name: Full reptend primes (Artin's conjecture for base 10)
results.usually_credited_to: Known since Lambert/Euler/Gauss; Gauss DA art. 315-317

deep.surprise_reason: This is a working continuation of the index and decimal-period tables that Gauss published, in this same normalization, in the Disquisitiones. The rest of the page is doodles, name trials and a Latin tag. The only mild interest is documentary: the early title 'Tentamen theoriae residuorum' and a draft table extending past 199.

checkable.asserts: Row 211: base 7 is a primitive root with 7^7 ≡ 10 and b = 210/30 = 7.
Row 223: 10 is a primitive root and ind_10(2) = 18.
The '*1' rows are exactly the primes in range having 10 as primitive root.
Each listed base g satisfies g^b ≡ 10 mod p.

transcription_corrections: The left column has the format 'p . g . b | ind_g(2)'. For example '211. 7.7 | 139' means p = 211, g = 7, b = 7, ind 2 = 139.
Row '359.399.2': the base cannot be 399 (> p), so the middle number needs re-reading from the image.
Row '331.37.3': the reading 37 is confirmed by computation (37^3 ≡ 10 mod 331, b = 3).
'13.3.2.4' in the margin is possibly '13.3.3.4' (ord_13(3) = 3, 12/3 = 4), by analogy with '11.5.3.2' (ord_11(3) = 5, 10/5 = 2). This is uncertain.
'Gauss eis' is upside-down pen-trial lettering, not mathematics.
